description: Learn why LeashFree.ca built a dog food comparison tool for Canadian dog owners and how it compares label-based nutrition, ingredients, calories, and estimated cost.
body:
Choosing dog food should be easier.

For many dog owners, comparing dog food brands can quickly become overwhelming. One bag says "high protein." Another says "grain-free." Another looks more affordable until you compare the bag size, calorie density, and feeding amount.

That is why we built the LeashFree.ca Dog Food Comparison Tool.

Our new tool helps Canadian dog owners compare dog food products side by side using practical, label-based information like nutrition, ingredients, calories, package size, and estimated cost. It is not about telling you which food is "best." It is about helping you compare available information more clearly.

Why we built this tool

LeashFree.ca started as a directory for leash-free dog parks across Canada, but our mission has always been broader than helping dog owners find places to walk their dogs.

We want LeashFree.ca to become a practical resource for Canadian dog owners. That means supporting more of the everyday decisions that come with caring for a dog, including where to exercise, how to understand breed needs, how to compare food options, and how to make care decisions with more confidence.

Dog food is one of the biggest recurring expenses for dog owners, and it is also one of the hardest things to compare fairly. A $95 bag is not automatically more expensive than a $70 bag. It depends on package size, calories per kilogram, and how long the food actually lasts.

What the Dog Food Comparison Tool does

The tool lets you select 2 to 4 dog foods and compare them side by side.

It looks at key information such as brand, product name, food type, life stage, main protein sources, grain-free or grain-inclusive status, guaranteed analysis, dry-matter protein, dry-matter fat, calories, package size, listed price, cost per kilogram, cost per 1,000 calories, estimated daily feeding cost, first five ingredients, ingredient flags, Made in Canada claims, and source or price-check dates.

Instead of making subjective claims, the tool highlights clear, measurable differences. For example, it may show which selected food has the lowest estimated daily cost, highest dry-matter protein, lowest dry-matter fat, highest calorie density, or a clearly different ingredient flag such as chicken-free, pea-free, grain-free, or grain-inclusive.

Why cost per bag is not enough

The price on the bag does not tell the full story. Two foods can have very different bag sizes, calorie density, feeding amounts, cost per kilogram, and cost per calorie.

That means one food may look cheaper upfront but cost more over time. Our tool calculates estimated values such as cost per kilogram, cost per 1,000 calories, and estimated daily cost based on a selected dog calorie amount.

These calculations are estimates, but they help compare foods more fairly than price alone.

Why we use dry-matter nutrition

Dog food labels usually show nutrition on an "as-fed" basis. That means the nutrition values include moisture.

This can make it difficult to compare products fairly, especially when comparing foods with different moisture levels. Our tool calculates dry-matter values for key nutrients like protein, fat, and fibre where the data is available.

By showing both the label value and the dry-matter value, the comparison uses a more consistent approach.

Built for Canadian dog owners

This tool is built specifically with Canadian dog owners in mind. Many dog food comparison articles include products, prices, or retailers that may not be relevant in Canada.

Our dataset focuses on dog foods commonly available to Canadian shoppers, including Canadian brands, Canadian-made foods, major retail brands, puppy foods, adult foods, senior foods, large-breed foods, grain-free recipes, and grain-inclusive recipes.

We also include source and price-check information so users can understand where the data came from and when it was last reviewed.

Who this tool is built for

The Dog Food Comparison Tool is built for dog owners who want a clearer way to compare food options.

  • New dog owners: Compare common products in a structured way when the number of options feels overwhelming.
  • Budget-conscious dog owners: Compare estimated daily cost instead of relying only on the sticker price.
  • Owners comparing brands: Review foods from brands such as ACANA, ORIJEN, FirstMate, Open Farm, Purina Pro Plan, Royal Canin, Hill's Science Diet, Performatrin, and others.
  • Owners watching ingredients: Spot listed ingredients such as chicken, beef, wheat, corn, soy, peas, lentils, or potatoes.
  • Owners of puppies, seniors, or large-breed dogs: Compare formulas by life stage and product type.
  • Research-minded dog owners: Review structured nutrition, ingredient, calorie, and price data instead of relying only on marketing copy.

What this tool is not

The LeashFree.ca Dog Food Comparison Tool is not veterinary advice. It does not diagnose health issues, recommend a medical diet, claim that one food is the healthiest, or replace advice from your veterinarian.

Every dog is different. Age, breed, size, activity level, health history, sensitivities, and body condition can all affect what food may be appropriate.

If your dog has a health condition, digestive issue, allergy concern, weight issue, or special nutritional need, speak with your veterinarian before changing foods.

Why we highlight differences with clear rules

One of the most important decisions we made was to avoid opinion-based scoring. You will not see a "food score" or a ranking based on unclear criteria.

Instead, the tool highlights measurable differences using clear rules. A protein highlight only appears when the difference is meaningful. A cost highlight only appears when the selected food is clearly lower in cost. Ingredient highlights appear when one selected food clearly differs from the others. Missing or older price data is shown as something to check.

The comparison is based on the data available, not hidden opinions.

Why accuracy matters

Dog food data can be tricky. Ingredients can change. Prices can change. Retailers may list different bag sizes. Some brands provide more complete nutrition data than others.

That is why we built a data-quality process behind the tool. Each product includes structured fields for nutrition, calories, ingredients, price, package size, sources, and review dates. We also use validation checks to catch missing data, duplicate products, stale prices, and incomplete records before they appear publicly.

What is included today

The first version includes a growing dataset of dry dog foods available in Canada. Current brands include ACANA, ORIJEN, FirstMate, Open Farm, GO! Solutions, NOW Fresh, Nutrience, Canadian Naturals, Boréal, Purina ONE, Purina Pro Plan, Royal Canin, Hill's Science Diet, IAMS, Pedigree, Blue Buffalo, Performatrin, Nutro, Wellness, Eukanuba, and Beneful.

We started with dry dog food because it is one of the most common formats purchased by Canadian dog owners and is easier to compare consistently by package size, calories, and daily cost.

Over time, we may expand into other food types, such as wet food, freeze-dried food, fresh food, or raw food, once we can support those comparisons accurately.

Our long-term goal

Our goal is to make LeashFree.ca more than a dog park directory. We want it to become a practical dog ownership resource for Canadians.

The Dog Food Comparison Tool is one step in that direction. It gives dog owners a better way to compare food options using structured information instead of relying only on marketing claims, package design, or price tags.

As we continue improving the tool, we plan to add more Canadian-market dog foods, better filters, more life-stage comparisons, improved ingredient search, clearer price freshness indicators, helpful educational content, and possibly user-requested foods for future review.

The LeashFree.ca Dog Food Comparison Tool helps you review nutrition, ingredients, calories, and price in one place so you can make a more informed decision for your dog.

name: How Many Calories Should My Dog Eat Per Day?
title: How Many Calories Should My Dog Eat Per Day?
seoTitle: How Many Calories Should My Dog Eat Per Day?
metaDescription: Learn how to estimate your dog's daily calorie needs using RER and MER, then use our dog calorie calculator to turn weight, activity, and life stage into a daily kcal target.
description: Learn how to estimate your dog's daily calorie needs using RER and MER, then use our dog calorie calculator to turn weight, activity, and life stage into a daily kcal target.
body:
Why Dog Calories Matter

Your dog's calorie needs affect more than body weight alone. The right amount helps support energy, muscle condition, digestion, mobility, and long-term health.

Too many calories over time can lead to weight gain and added stress on joints. Too few calories can leave a dog under-fuelled or nutritionally short if portions are cut too far.

The goal is not a perfect fixed number forever. The goal is a strong starting point, regular check-ins, and gradual adjustments based on body condition.

The Difference Between RER and MER

Most calorie estimates start with two key terms: RER and MER.

RER means Resting Energy Requirement. It estimates calories needed for basic body functions at rest.

Common formula: RER = 70 ? body weight in kg^0.75

MER means Maintenance Energy Requirement. It adjusts RER for real-life factors like activity level, life stage, neuter status, growth, and weight goals.

In simple terms: MER = RER ? life-stage or activity factor

That MER value is your estimated daily calorie target.

What Affects Your Dog's Daily Calorie Needs?

Two dogs with the same weight may need different calorie amounts. Needs can vary by age, activity level, ideal weight, body type, metabolism, health status, and lifestyle.

  • Age and life stage
  • Current and ideal weight
  • Activity level
  • Spay/neuter status
  • Breed and body composition
  • Medical conditions
  • Pregnancy or nursing
  • Climate and daily routine

For example, an active young dog may need far more calories than a sedentary senior of the same size. Puppies also need more calories per pound than most adults because they are still growing.

How to Use a Dog Calorie Calculator

To estimate your dog's calories, enter weight, life stage, activity level, and goal (maintain, lose, or gain). Our Dog Calorie Calculator then returns an estimated daily target in kcal/day.

Remember this target includes everything your dog eats in a day: meals, treats, chews, toppers, and training rewards.

How to Convert Calories Into Food Amount

Once you have a daily calorie target, use the calorie information on your dog food label:

  • kcal per cup
  • kcal per can
  • kcal per 100 g
  • kcal per kg

Then convert:

  • Cups/day = daily kcal target ? kcal per cup
  • Cans/day = daily kcal target ? kcal per can
  • Grams/day = daily kcal target ? kcal per gram

Example: if your dog needs 600 kcal/day and food provides 400 kcal/cup, then 600 ? 400 = 1.5 cups/day (0.75 cups per meal if feeding twice daily).

For better consistency, use a kitchen scale when possible.

Should Dogs Eat Once or Twice a Day?

Most adult dogs do well with two meals per day. Some do fine with one, while others do better with smaller, more frequent feedings.

Puppies usually need three to four smaller meals daily, especially at younger stages. Dogs with medical or digestive needs may require a custom schedule from a veterinarian.

How to Tell If the Calorie Target Is Working

A calculator gives a starting estimate, but body condition confirms whether intake is right.

  • Ribs should be easy to feel without being sharply visible
  • A visible waist should be present from above
  • A slight abdominal tuck should be visible from the side
  • Energy should remain steady

After portion changes, reassess after 1 to 2 weeks. If weight change is too fast, adjust by about 5 to 10 percent and reassess.

Can You Use a Dog Calorie Calculator for Weight Loss?

Yes, with care. If a dog is overweight, targets are often based on ideal weight rather than current weight. Weight loss should be gradual and nutritionally complete.

Avoid aggressive food cuts that can increase hunger and reduce nutrient intake. For significant weight loss, veterinary guidance is recommended.

Feeding by Calories vs Feeding by Cups

Calories are usually more accurate than cups because foods vary in energy density. A cup is volume, not nutrition.

Tracking by calories also helps account for treats. If your dog needs 700 kcal/day and gets 100 kcal from treats, meals should provide about 600 kcal that day.

Common Mistakes When Estimating Dog Calories

  • Forgetting to count treats and extras
  • Treating bag feeding guides as fixed rules
  • Not recalculating after lifestyle or life-stage changes
  • Making large feeding changes too quickly

When to Ask Your Veterinarian

A calculator is useful, but it does not replace veterinary care. Ask your veterinarian if your dog is a fast-growing puppy, pregnant, nursing, underweight, overweight, a senior with appetite changes, on a prescription diet, or showing unexpected weight change.

Calculate Your Dog's Daily Calories

Use our free Dog Calorie Calculator to estimate kcal/day from weight, activity level, and life stage.

Use the result as a starting point, monitor body condition, and adjust gradually over time.

FAQ

How many calories should my dog eat per day?

It depends on weight, age, activity, body condition, and health status. A calorie calculator using RER and MER is the easiest place to start.

What does kcal mean on dog food?

Kcal means kilocalories. On pet food labels, kcal is the same unit commonly called Calories.

Should I feed my dog based on calories or cups?

Calories are more accurate because cup volume can hide large differences in food density across brands and formulas.

Do treats count toward my dog's daily calories?

Yes. Treats, chews, toppers, scraps, and training rewards all count toward total daily intake.

How often should I recalculate my dog's calories?

Recalculate when weight, activity, life stage, health status, or diet changes. Recheck every few weeks during active weight management.

Can puppies use a dog calorie calculator?

Yes, but puppies have different growth needs. Use a puppy setting and consult your veterinarian, especially for large-breed puppies.

Not sure how many calories your dog needs?
Use our free Dog Calorie Calculator to estimate a daily kcal target based on weight, activity level, and life stage.

name: How Hot Is Too Hot to Walk a Dog in Canada?
title: How Hot Is Too Hot to Walk a Dog in Canada?
seoTitle: How Hot Is Too Hot to Walk a Dog in Canada? | LeashFree.ca
metaDescription: Learn when it is too hot to walk your dog in Canada, how to check pavement, spot heatstroke signs, protect paws, and plan safer summer walks in extreme heat.
description: Hot pavement, humidity, and extreme heat can make dog walks unsafe. Learn when to shorten or skip a walk, how to check pavement, and safer summer options.
body:
Quick Answer

There is no single temperature that makes every dog walk safe or unsafe. Heat risk depends on air temperature, humidity, direct sun, pavement temperature, shade, wind, your dog's breed, age, coat, fitness, and health.

As a practical Canadian summer rule, start being cautious around 24 C, shorten walks around 27 C to 31 C, and skip non-essential walks when it is 32 C or hotter, especially if it is humid or sunny.

On extreme heat days, think of the walk as a quick potty break, not exercise. Use shade, grass, water, and early morning or late evening timing.

A Simple Heat Guide for Dog Walks

Use this as a general planning guide, not veterinary advice. If your dog has health issues, is very young or senior, has a short muzzle, or overheats easily, be more conservative.

  • Under 20 C: Usually comfortable for many healthy dogs, assuming the pavement is not hot and the dog is not overexerted.
  • 20 C to 23 C: Still manageable for many dogs, but watch direct sun, humidity, and dark pavement.
  • 24 C to 27 C: Use caution. Choose shade, grass, water breaks, and shorter walks.
  • 28 C to 31 C: High caution. Avoid hard exercise, walk early or late, and consider indoor enrichment instead.
  • 32 C and above: Skip non-essential walks. Keep outings short and focused on bathroom breaks.

The number on your weather app is only part of the picture. Asphalt, concrete, artificial turf, poor airflow, and humid conditions can make a normal-looking walk much harder on your dog.

Why Hot Walks Are Risky for Dogs

Dogs do not cool themselves the way people do. They rely heavily on panting, limited sweating through their paw pads, shade, cooler surfaces, and rest.

That means a dog can overheat faster than an owner expects, especially when they are excited, pulling, running, playing fetch, or walking on hot pavement.

Heat can also build up before a dog looks distressed. By the time a dog is frantic, weak, vomiting, confused, or collapsing, the situation is urgent.

The Pavement Test

Paw burns are one of the easiest summer hazards to miss. Pavement can be far hotter than the air, especially in direct sun.

Before walking on asphalt, concrete, boardwalks, or artificial turf, place the back of your hand or palm on the surface for several seconds. If it is uncomfortable for you, it is too hot for your dog's paws.

When in doubt, move to grass, dirt trails, shaded paths, or delay the walk. Dog boots can help some dogs, but they are not a licence to exercise hard in heat. Boots also need to fit properly, and some dogs overheat faster when gear traps warmth.

Humidity Changes the Risk

Canadian summer heat is not the same everywhere. A dry 28 C day in Calgary can feel very different from a humid 28 C day in Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal, Halifax, or Windsor.

Humidity makes panting less effective. If the air already feels heavy, sticky, and hard to breathe, your dog may struggle to cool down even during a moderate walk.

On humid days, reduce distance, slow the pace, stay close to home, and avoid long off-leash sessions at the dog park.

Dogs That Need Extra Caution

Some dogs are more vulnerable in summer heat. Be extra conservative with:

  • Flat-faced breeds such as bulldogs, French bulldogs, pugs, boxers, and shih tzus
  • Senior dogs

body:
Quick Answer

Pet insurance can be useful for Canadian dog owners, but the best policy is not always the cheapest monthly premium. Before you buy, compare the deductible, reimbursement rate, annual limit, waiting periods, exclusions, dental rules, direct-vet-pay options, renewal terms, and how the policy treats pre-existing conditions.

The strongest plan is the one that fits your dog, your savings, and the type of bill that would actually hurt your household. A healthy puppy, a senior dog, a flat-faced breed, a giant breed, and an active off-leash dog may all need different coverage choices.

LeashFree.ca is not an insurer, broker, veterinarian, or financial advisor. This guide is a practical comparison worksheet for dog owners. Always read the current policy wording and ask the provider specific questions before enrolling.

Why This Matters for Canadian Dog Owners

Dog ownership in Canada is expensive enough when everything goes well. Food, routine vet care, grooming, parasite prevention, licensing, training, and gear already create a meaningful annual budget. The harder problem is the bill you cannot schedule: a swallowed object, torn ligament, emergency imaging, dental trauma, cancer workup, or overnight hospitalization.

That is the real job of pet insurance. It does not make vet care free. It helps convert some large, unpredictable, eligible bills into a more manageable monthly premium plus your share of the claim.

If you are still deciding whether insurance belongs in your plan, start with our Is Dog Insurance Worth It in Canada? guide and the Dog Cost Calculator Canada. Then use this article to compare policies line by line.

How Pet Insurance Usually Works

Most dog insurance policies are reimbursement-based. You pay the vet, submit a claim, and the insurer reimburses eligible costs based on the policy terms. Some providers may offer direct payment to participating clinics, but you should confirm how that works before counting on it in an emergency.

The core terms are:

  • Premium: The monthly or annual price of the policy.
  • Deductible: The amount you pay before reimbursement applies. This may be annual or per-condition.
  • Reimbursement rate: The percentage of eligible costs the insurer pays after the deductible, often shown as 70%, 80%, or 90%.
  • Annual limit: The maximum the insurer will pay in a policy year.
  • Exclusions: Conditions, treatments, fees, or situations the policy does not cover.
  • Waiting period: The time after enrollment before coverage starts for accidents, illnesses, orthopedic conditions, or other categories.

A policy with a low monthly premium can still be expensive if the deductible is high, the reimbursement rate is low, the annual limit is small, or the exclusions remove the conditions you care about most.

The 10 Things To Compare Before You Buy

Use this table when comparing Canadian pet insurance providers. Do not rely on the quote page alone. Open the sample policy, policy wording, certificate, or coverage summary.

Pet Insurance Comparison Checklist

Feature What to check Why it matters
Annual limitPer-year cap such as $5,000, $10,000, $20,000, or unlimitedA low cap may run out during a major illness or multi-visit year.
Deductible typeAnnual vs per-condition; amount optionsPer-condition deductibles can behave very differently from annual deductibles.
Reimbursement rate70%, 80%, 90%, or another amountThis determines how much of each eligible bill remains yours.
Waiting periodsAccident, illness, orthopedic, dental, or special-condition waitsClaims during the waiting period are usually not eligible.
Pre-existing conditionsDefinition, symptom lookback, curable-condition rulesA symptom before enrollment can affect future coverage.
Dental coverageDental illness, trauma, extractions, routine cleaningDental wording varies a lot and routine cleaning is often treated separately.
Exam fees and taxesWhether consultation fees, exam fees, and taxes are eligibleThese can be a real part of the bill even when treatment is covered.
Alternative and rehab carePhysiotherapy, hydrotherapy, acupuncture, chiropractic, behavioural supportUseful for orthopedic recovery, injury rehab, and some chronic cases.
Direct vet paymentAvailable clinics, approval process, emergency limitationsReimbursement later is not the same as avoiding a large upfront payment.
Renewal and price changesAge increases, regional pricing, claim history, policy changesA policy you can afford at age two may cost more at age eight.

Quick Answer

If your dog may need emergency care, call a veterinarian or 24/7 emergency clinic first, then get moving if they tell you to come in. Do not wait at home trying to price-shop if your dog is struggling to breathe, collapsing, bleeding heavily, having repeated seizures, showing signs of bloat, or may have eaten something toxic.

The money side still matters. The best time to prepare is before the crisis. Save your nearest emergency clinics, know how you would pay the deposit, understand your pet insurance claim process, and keep a one-page medical summary for your dog.

The 3-Minute Emergency Vet Bill Checklist

Use this first when you are stressed and need the shortest possible plan.

Emergency Vet Bill Checklist

Step What to do Why it matters
1Call your vet or nearest emergency clinic.They can triage and tell you whether to come in now.
2If breathing, collapse, major bleeding, toxin exposure, bloat signs, or repeated seizures are involved, treat it as urgent.Delay can change the medical outcome and final cost.
3Bring medication names, insurance details, ID, and a payment method.Clinics often need consent and a deposit before treatment proceeds.
4Ask for an estimate with low, likely, and high ranges.Emergency care can change as test results arrive.
5After discharge, save the invoice and medical records for insurance or your emergency fund tracking.Clean records make claims and follow-up care easier.

description: Learn how to compare dog food cost per day in Canada using calories, package size, and feeding amount. Includes real dry-food examples and a fair method for kibble, wet, fresh, and raw food.
body:
Quick Answer

The fairest way to compare dog food cost in Canada is not by bag price. It is by cost per 1,000 kcal and then by estimated daily feeding cost for your dog.

That matters because kibble, wet food, fresh food, and raw food can have very different moisture levels, calorie density, package sizes, and feeding amounts. A cheaper-looking bag or box can cost more per day once you compare the calories you actually get.

For most healthy adult dogs, the best workflow is simple: estimate your dog's daily calorie target, find the food's kcal value from the label, convert that into a daily portion, and then calculate the cost. Use the Dog Calorie Calculator, the Dog Food Comparison Tool Canada, and the Dog Cost Calculator Canada together.

What Actually Determines Dog Food Cost Per Day

Four things drive daily food cost more than the sticker price:

  • Calories per kilogram: Higher-calorie foods may require a smaller daily portion.
  • Package size: A cheaper bag may also be much smaller.
  • Your dog's calorie needs: A 10 kg dog and a 35 kg dog are not eating the same amount.
  • Food format: Dry, wet, fresh, and raw foods often carry very different moisture levels and packaging costs.

This is why “price per bag” and even “price per kilogram” can mislead. Cost per kilogram is more useful than sticker price, but it still misses calorie density. Cost per 1,000 kcal is usually the better comparison baseline.

The 4 Numbers To Compare

Dog Food Cost Comparison Metrics

Metric Formula Why it matters
Cost per kg Price / package kg Good first pass, but does not account for calorie density.
Cost per 1,000 kcal Price / (package kcal / 1,000) Best cross-product cost comparison for most foods.
Daily portion Daily kcal target / food kcal value Shows how much of that specific food your dog may eat.
Daily cost Cost per 1,000 kcal x (daily kcal / 1,000) Turns label math into a real budget number.

Four things drive daily food cost more than the sticker price:

  • Calories per kilogram: Higher-calorie foods may require a smaller daily portion.
  • Package size: A cheaper bag may also be much smaller.
  • Your dog's calorie needs: A 10 kg dog and a 35 kg dog are not eating the same amount.
  • Food format: Dry, wet, fresh, and raw foods often carry very different moisture levels and packaging costs.

This is why “price per bag” and even “price per kilogram” can mislead. Cost per kilogram is more useful than sticker price, but it still misses calorie density. Cost per 1,000 kcal is usually the better comparison baseline.

The 4 Numbers To Compare

Dog Food Cost Comparison Metrics

Metric Formula Why it matters
Cost per kg Price / package kg Good first pass, but does not account for calorie density.
Cost per 1,000 kcal Price / (package kcal / 1,000) Best cross-product cost comparison for most foods.
Daily portion Daily kcal target / food kcal value Shows how much of that specific food your dog may eat.
Daily cost Cost per 1,000 kcal x (daily kcal / 1,000) Turns label math into a real budget number.
